issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: 'Risky Behavior' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which otherwise emphasizes hypervigilance, startle, danger in silence, fragmented/avoided trauma memory, and appraisals of betrayal and injustice after police violence. Those other items describe a fearful, threat-sensitive presentation; endorsing active risk-taking as a core threat item pulls in the opposite direction and is not supported elsewhere in the selected nodes.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself
issues.explanation: 'Can't Rely on Self' is a weaker fit than the other appraisals for this trauma/context. The profile is organized around external betrayal/injustice linked to police violence, but this item shifts to global self-distrust without corresponding self-blame, shame, incompetence, or strategy items elsewhere. In combination with the strong betrayal/injustice theme, it creates a less coherent appraisal profile.

vignette:
Miguel is a 54-year-old parole officer who has spent nearly three decades supervising men and women released back into the community. Married for twenty-two years, he lives with his wife in a quiet suburban neighborhood outside a midsized city in the Southwest. What brought him to treatment was a single event that now feels like an unfinished story he can neither finish telling nor shake.

It happened eighteen months ago during a joint operation with a local police tactical team. Miguel was present as the parole liaison for a high-risk arrest, standing off to the side in the predawn dark. He had worked with this particular unit for years, considered several of the officers friends. The suspect was believed to be armed, and the team moved in with the usual controlled chaos. But something went wrong. An officer Miguel had trusted—had shared meals with, had joked with about the job—suddenly swung and struck him across the face with the butt of a rifle. The blow came without warning, without any command or provocation. Miguel dropped to his knees, blood streaming from a split brow, and as he looked up he saw the officer’s eyes: wide, panicked, as if he had mistaken Miguel for the target. The operation continued around him, and it was several minutes before anyone helped him to his feet. The official report later described the incident as a “friendly fire accident” and the officer was placed on administrative leave for two weeks before returning to duty. No charges were filed. No apology was offered. The department’s internal investigation concluded that the officer had acted reasonably under the stress of the moment.

Miguel’s memory of that morning is fragmented. He can recall the cold metal of the rifle stock, the shock of impact, the taste of blood. But there are gaps. He finds himself pushing the memory away before it fully forms, as if his mind slams a door on the image before he can see what comes next. When he tries to tell the story to his wife or his therapist, it sounds hollow, unreal—like a movie scene that could not possibly have happened to him. He knows it did, but the memory carries a quality of disbelief that leaves him doubting his own experience.

In the months that followed, Miguel began to change in ways he did not fully recognize at first. At work, he started noticing the small things: a parolee arriving late, a tense tone of voice, a missed check-in. These “misbehaviors,” as he calls them, trigger a surge of adrenaline that feels out of proportion. He finds himself scanning every room he enters—the waiting area at the parole office, the lobby of the courthouse, even the grocery store on a Saturday morning. He looks for exits, for people who are standing too still, for the kind of unusual silence that, to him, now feels like the moment before a blow lands. When a room goes quiet, his chest tightens and he is certain something dangerous is about to happen. He startles easily: a car backfiring on the street makes him drop his keys; someone touching his shoulder from behind sends him spinning around with his fists clenched.

His own body has become a trigger. When he is stressed—and he is stressed most of the time now—his heart begins to pound. The sensation of his own racing heart, the thudding in his chest, immediately transports him back to those seconds on the ground, waiting for the next blow. He has come to interpret that physical feeling as a sign that something terrible is imminent, and so he tries to avoid stress altogether, which is impossible in his line of work.

Avoidance crept into his daily life slowly. He stopped volunteering for joint operations with police. He began leaving work exactly at five, refusing to take after-hours calls. He stopped meeting colleagues for coffee after shift, telling himself he was too tired. At home, he grew quiet. His wife noticed he no longer wanted to watch the news, especially any report about police conduct or use of force. He would leave the room if a discussion turned to law enforcement accountability. On weekends, he found reasons to stay inside—organizing the garage, mowing the lawn—anything to avoid the unpredictable social world outside. He has not spoken to the officer who struck him, and he avoids any gathering where that officer might be present, which means he has skipped three department retreats and one retirement party. His supervisor has noticed. Last month, Miguel received a written warning about his “lack of collaboration” with interagency teams.

What weighs on Miguel most heavily, though, is not the avoidance or the hypervigilance. It is the sense of betrayal that has calcified in his chest. He trusted that officer. He trusted the institution that trained them both. And when nothing was done—when the investigation concluded with a shrug and a two-week suspension—something in him broke. He believes what happened to him was deeply unfair, and that the people who should have protected him instead covered for one of their own. This injustice is a raw nerve that twitches every time he puts on his badge. He still wears it, but it no longer feels like it belongs to him.

Miguel came to therapy because his wife finally told him she was afraid of the man he was becoming—distant, irritable, always on edge. He is afraid too, though he would not have said so at first. What he hopes is that someone can help him make the memory feel real enough to face, so that maybe then he can stop scanning for a danger that, for eighteen months, has never come.
